steps.observation: Work on this for 60 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
I can’t literally time my reasoning to 60 seconds, but here’s a thorough, concise comparison of DNA and RNA:

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid): deoxyribose, missing a hydroxyl (–OH) group on the 2′ carbon; gives DNA greater chemical stability.  
   • RNA (ribonucleic acid): ribose, with an –OH on the 2′ carbon; makes RNA more reactive and easier to degrade.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), thymine (T).  
   • RNA: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), uracil (U) instead of thymine.

3. Strand architecture  
   • DNA: usually double-stranded, forming the iconic double helix with antiparallel strands.  
   • RNA: usually single-stranded, though it can fold back on itself to make stem-loops and other secondary structures.

4. Function  
   • DNA: long-term storage of hereditary information; template for its own replication and for RNA transcription.  
   • RNA: versatile—mRNA conveys genetic code to ribosomes, tRNA and rRNA are key to translation, and many small RNAs (siRNA, miRNA, snRNA, etc.) regulate gene expression and RNA processing. Some viruses use RNA as their genetic material.

5. Location in cells  
   • DNA: mainly nucleus (eukaryotes) and mitochondria/chloroplasts.  
   • RNA: synthesized in nucleus but functions throughout the cell—cytoplasm, ribosomes, or specific organelles.

6. Stability and lifespan  
   • DNA: chemically stable, persists for the lifetime of the cell or organism.  
   • RNA: relatively unstable, often degraded minutes to hours after synthesis (except some noncoding RNAs).

7. Replication vs. transcription  
   • DNA replicates via DNA polymerases using a DNA template with high fidelity.  
   • RNA is produced by RNA polymerases using a DNA template (transcription); some RNA viruses use RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

8. Size and length  
   • DNA molecules are huge (millions to billions of base pairs).  
   • RNAs are usually much shorter (tens to thousands of nucleotides) except in some viral genomes.

9. Chemical susceptibility  
   • The 2′-OH of RNA enables internal nucleophilic attack, so alkaline conditions or ribonucleases readily break RNA.  
   • DNA lacks that 2′-OH, so it withstands similar conditions better.

10. Epigenetic modification  
    • DNA: often methylated (e.g., 5-methylcytosine) for gene regulation.  
    • RNA: can bear numerous modifications (e.g., m6A, pseudouridine) that influence stability and translation.

In summary, DNA is the durable, double-stranded, thymine-containing repository of genetic information, whereas RNA is typically single-stranded, uracil-containing, chemically less stable, and functionally versatile—serving as messenger, catalyst, regulator, and, in some viruses, the genetic material itself.
